speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment under the proposed beverage container return scheme (a) what are the types of pre-packaged beverage or container envisaged to be included; (b) what are the annual projected costs and expenditure to run the scheme; and (c) what are the Ministry's plans to utilise any excess deposit or fees which remain un-refunded because of beverage containers not returned.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The proposed beverage container return scheme aims to encourage good recycling practices, conserve resources and reduce waste and carbon emissions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is in line with our Zero Waste Masterplan and contributes towards our climate ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by or around mid-century.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The scheme, which was first proposed by the Citizens' Workgroup on #RecycleRight in 2019, will be the first phase of an Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) approach to manage packaging waste.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This Extended Producer Responsibility approach means that the scheme will be funded by producers of pre-packaged beverages.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under the EPR approach, beverage producers, such as manufacturers and importers, will be responsible for the collection and recycling of the products they put out on the market as well as funding the scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is similar to the EPR scheme that was implemented for e-waste in 2021.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Under the beverage container return scheme, a small refundable deposit will be applied when a consumer buys a pre-packaged beverage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I must emphasise that this is a refundable deposit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Consumers will get a full refund of their deposits when they return their empty beverage containers at designated return points.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Compared to non-deposit-based recycling schemes, the refundable deposit will encourage a higher recycling rate and aggregate a stream of cleaner and higher quality recyclables that can be used to produce new products, thus enhancing the resource loop.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similar schemes in countries such as Norway, Sweden and Lithuania, have achieved return rates of 80% or higher.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Producers typically appoint an operator to carry out their responsibilities under the scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Based on the experience of other countries, a not-for-profit, industry-led scheme operator is preferred.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It will be able to tap on the industry's capabilities and resources, such as existing logistics channels to make use of backhaul trips to improve operational synergies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As the scheme is owned and run by the industry, it will have a strong incentive to operate the scheme efficiently and cost-effectively, to keep scheme costs low for all parties.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, the revenue from the sale of clean, high quality and high value recyclables, and any unclaimed deposits, will be utilised by the scheme operator to reduce the scheme costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In Singapore, the eventual cost pass-through to consumers in beverage prices, if any, will likely be moderated by price competition among industry players.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is also the experience in other countries that have implemented similar schemes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To ensure that the scheme operator operates efficiently, cost effectively and fairly across multiple producers, the Government will exercise regulatory oversight over the scheme operator.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The scheme operator will be licensed by NEA and be required to meet conditions set out by NEA, including a collection target.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To develop the scheme framework for Singapore, my Ministry and NEA have conducted over two years of extensive engagements and consultations with stakeholders, including members of the public and over 250 beverage producers, retailers and waste management companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have taken into account their feedback and views in developing a proposed scheme framework, and we are currently conducting further public consultation via REACH.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As public consultations are still ongoing, not all the details of the scheme have been finalised.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are proposing for the scheme to cover plastic bottles and metal cans as a start, as these have high material value, high consumption rates and are easy to collect and compact.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also propose to include all beverage types to reduce consumer confusion and maximise the number of containers that can be collected for recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The scheme would include containers from 150 millilitres to three litres, which can be accepted by typical reverse vending machines.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In designing the scheme, we will make it easy for consumers to understand, to enable each of us to play our part in building a circular economy.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will need to have an extensive network of conveniently located return points to enable consumers to easily claim their deposit refunds.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We also welcome operators of other premises, such as mall operators and smaller retailers, to voluntarily set up return points.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Based on experiences overseas, this can increase footfall to stores.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The scheme operator pays handling fees to return point operators, to reimburse the costs incurred.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To build the return point network, NEA will work closely with the future scheme operator to identify and set up return points in suitable community and public spaces, such as Community Clubs, sports facilities and large, well-patronised hawker centres, to increase accessibility.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Return point operators can choose manual over-the-counter return points or opt for automated reverse vending machines.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: At food and beverage (F&B) premises, such as hawker centres, food courts and canteens, operators and stallholders have the flexibility to decide whether to collect the deposit and pass the beverage containers to their patrons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There is a wide range of such premises, from casual settings to more formal settings, and each would have its own preference.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Alternatively, stallholders could pour the beverage into a cup before serving, in which case, they do not need to charge the deposit as the customer does not receive the beverage container.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In this case, the stallholder can collect the empty beverage containers and claim the refund of the deposits on the containers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We expect the former to apply in more casual settings, such as coffee shops and hawker centres, as the shop owners would typically have their customers pay the deposit and then take the beverage container.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Operators of F&B premises, including hawker centres, food courts and canteens, could also consider setting up return points at their premises, where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: NEA will work with the scheme operator to engage F&B premises operators, advise them on the scheme and prepare them for implementation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will continue to engage stakeholders as we develop the scheme.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My supplementary question is in relation to continuing cost-benefit analysis for this scheme.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2001, Israel introduced a deposit refund law for glass and plastic containers smaller than 1.5 litres.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A cost-benefit analysis in 2010 was done and it concluded that the law had a positive impact, with total benefits exceeding total cost by around 35%.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the same vein, can the Senior Minister of State and the Ministry also consider a similar cost-benefit analysis, and a regular reporting can be done on the effectiveness of the scheme, including possible recommendations of expansion of the scheme, if that is beneficial?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I think it is, indeed, important that we do this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to challenges, as I have alluded to, in order to facilitate return of the beverage containers, which is really the key objective of this scheme, that is, to nudge consumers' behaviour, nudge them to recycle the beverage containers, we will need to have an extensive network of return points to make it easily and conveniently accessible to the consumers, so that they can return and get back their deposit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For a start, we are mandating the large supermarkets above 200 square metres to have these return points because our survey and engagements with the public have shown that that is one of the most popular return point locations.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Of course, it is also the single largest sales channel for prepackaged beverages.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: About a third of the total sales volume of prepackaged beverages is through the supermarkets and there will be about 400 of them, which is about two-thirds of the number of supermarkets that we have in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But beyond that, we will be looking at working with the future scheme operator and other stakeholders to have designated return points at other locations, publicly accessible locations, such as Community Centres, Residents' Networks (RNs), void decks, sports facilities, hawker centres which are well-patronised or even coffee shops.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And, of course, some retailers, as is the experience in other countries do come forward to volunteer to have designated return points because that has been shown to increase footfall and, therefore, spending at the stores.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, we will implement this and then, monitor to see whether that is adequate and we can always refine this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I think that also answers the Member's question on return points, because this is one of the key issues.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Of course, the other thing is to keep the scheme cost low and we are doing this by encouraging the producers to come together to form a not-for-profit industry-led scheme operator, which means that they can actually tap on their existing logistics as well as distribution networks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, for instance, when they send new stocks, they can take back the used beverage containers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition to that, it is really a strong incentive since they are paying producers' fees to keep scheme costs low.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Then, the sale of the high-quality, high value recyclables will help to offset some of the costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to GST, based on the intended scheme design, GST will not be chargeable on the deposit.
